title: Matthew 21:18–22
context: The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, curses a leafy but fruitless fig tree, and teaches the marveling disciples about faith that does not doubt and prayer that receives—linking judgment on barren religion with a call to living trust.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On The morning after the temple confrontation, Jesus returns toward Jerusalem hungry, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The disciples seeing it - As they went by, the next day. Jesus answering, said, If ye have faith - Whence we may learn, that one great end of our Lord in this miracle was to confirm and increase their faith: another was, to warn them against unfruitfulness.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 21:18–22)

reformed.quote: Matthew says that the city was moved, in order to inform us that the transaction did not take place secretly, or by stealth, but in the presence of all the people, and that the priests and scribes were not ignorant of it. Under this despicable aspect of the flesh the majesty of the Spirit was apparent; for how would they have endured that Christ should be conducted into the city, attended by the splendor of royalty, with so great danger to themselves, if they had not been seized with astonishment?
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 21:18–22)

verses.text: Now in the morning, as he returned to the city, he was hungry.
verses.arminianNotes:
Morning finds Jesus returning to the city and genuinely hungry. The King’s true humanity frames what follows: need that seeks fruit, not a staged puzzle.

Arminians hear grace still moving toward Jerusalem. The One who cleansed the temple comes again; hunger becomes the occasion for a living parable about fruit and faith that disciples must take to heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Matthew notes the hour and Jesus’ hunger as He returns to the city. Ordinary need sits inside the Passion Week timetable.

Reformed readers see providence in the detail: the Son’s hunger is not accident but the appointed doorway to a sign. What follows will interpret fruitless religion under the Lord’s sovereign purpose.

verses.text: Seeing a fig tree by the road, he came to it and found nothing on it but leaves. He said to it, “Let there be no fruit from you forever!” Immediately the fig tree withered away.
verses.arminianNotes:
Leaves without fruit meet a word of judgment: “Let there be no fruit from you forever!” The tree withers at once—an acted warning against show without substance, echoing Israel’s temple leadership and fruitless religion.

Arminian pastoral reading hears a serious summons. Grace exposes barren profession and calls for living faith that bears fruit. Enabling grace is given so hearers may repent of leaf-only religion and become fruitful rather than wither under deserved warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jesus finds leaves only and pronounces a curse; the tree withers immediately. The sign judges appearance without fruit—aimed at fruitless Israel and temple religion under the King’s authority.

This is a judicial act within providence, not impulsive frustration. The Lord who rules creation and covenant history displays what barrenness receives; the withering is certain because His word and purpose stand.
verses.keyContrast: Both read the withered fig as judgment on fruitless religion tied to Israel and the temple motif. Arminians typically press an actual warning that presses repentance, with enabling grace toward fruitful faith; Reformed readers stress a judicial sign under providence—Christ’s authoritative sentence on barrenness advancing God’s purpose.

verses.text: When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree immediately wither away?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The disciples marvel and ask how the tree withered at once. Wonder is appropriate; the question opens them to Jesus’ teaching on faith.

Classical Arminians welcome honest amazement. Grace uses their surprise to draw them further—from spectacle to trust. The right response to the sign is not mere curiosity but readiness to learn what living faith and prayer require.
verses.reformedNotes:
Marvel and question mark the disciples’ response to the sudden withering. Jesus will interpret the sign for them.

God grants both the miracle and the teaching that follows. Their amazement is the appointed hinge; the Lord who withered the tree will also instruct His own about faith under His sovereign hand.

verses.text: Jesus answered them, “Most certainly I tell you, if you have faith and don’t doubt, you will not only do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you told this mountain, ‘Be taken up and cast into the sea,’ it would be done.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jesus answers with a solemn promise: faith that does not doubt can share in what was done to the fig tree—and even command a mountain into the sea. The call is to undivided trust, not half-hearted profession.

This is an invitation empowered by assisting grace. God enables believers to trust without wavering; mountain language presses confident reliance on Him. Faith is living response God strengthens, not empty bravado—fruitful because grace makes steadfast trust possible.
verses.reformedNotes:
“Most certainly I tell you” grounds mountain-moving faith in Jesus’ certain word. Faith without doubt is the instrument of God’s power, not human self-assertion.

Such faith is God’s gift, wrought by the Spirit. The promise does not hand sovereignty to the disciple; it assures that God works through true faith according to His purpose—removing what He wills, as surely as He withered the tree.
verses.keyContrast: Both take Jesus’ call to undoubting faith seriously. Arminians emphasize a grace-enabled trust believers are summoned to exercise; Calvinists typically emphasize faith as God’s gift and instrument—mountain-moving power according to His sovereign purpose, not independent human will.

verses.text: All things, whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The lesson widens to prayer: whatever you ask, you will receive, if you have faith. Asking is not in doubt; receiving is tied to trusting dependence on God.

Enabling grace sustains believing prayer. God sincerely invites His people to ask and receive; faith that leans on Him is met with the Father’s generosity. The warning of the fig tree and the promise of prayer together call for fruitful, living communion—not leafy unbelief.
verses.reformedNotes:
Prayer that receives is prayer of faith. “Whatever you ask” is held inside the larger biblical witness: God answers according to His will and glory.

Faith does not bend God to our whims; it aligns asking with the Father’s purpose. The Spirit grants both the faith and the prayers God intends to answer—so the promise comforts without turning prayer into a blank check outside providence.
verses.keyContrast: Both affirm that faith-filled prayer receives from God. Arminians stress a sincere invitation and enabling grace for asking that truly receives; Reformed interpreters underline prayer answered according to God’s will and purpose—faith itself the gift that asks within His sovereign design.
